sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2019. Is Sinyar an SBB language? Handout, 14th Nilo-Saharan Linguistics Colloquium, University of Vienna, 29 May - 1 June 2019. HAL halshs-04579988 (deposited 2024).
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Nothing for Mo'da. The handout's tone material (sec. 4 'Tone patterns as evidence for a substrate?', Tables 12-13 'SBB / Sinyar tones compared', 1=L 2=H) compares Sinyar with *SBB, Modo, Bongo, Gula Koto and Sar only; Mo'da figures solely in the lexicostatistic classification.

sources.citation: Boyeldieu, Pascal. 2016. Stratigraphie lexicale et renouvellement du vocabulaire dans les langues SBB 'occidentales' (Afrique centrale). Faits de Langues 47 (Comparaison et reconstruction: tendances actuelles): 125-150. HAL halshs-01487214.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: Nothing on Mo'da stress or tone. The paper reconstructs *SBB lexical strata; tone is discussed only for the reconstruction and for well-documented languages. For Mo'da it gives (i) a lexicostatistic placement in group D, (ii) a handful of untoned forms in the comparative tables (e.g. N/009 'feu': mo'da waɗʊ vs modo pàɗʊ̀, 'beli Wu pàɗʊ̀), and (iii) the documentary statement that only lists of at most 150 items exist for mo'da. It also announces 'Boyeldieu (en préparation), La classification des langues SBB orientales, essai de mise à jour', based on 'données tonales et lexicales nouvelles' --…

sources.citation: Baxter, P. T. W. & Audrey Butt. 1953. The Azande and Related Peoples of the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan and Belgian Congo (Ethnographic Survey of Africa, East Central Africa, Part IX). London: International African Institute. Part II 'The Bongo-Baka group', secs. 3-5 and 'Language'.
sources.tag: read: silent on stress
sources.note: No phonology content. Language remarks are classificatory only: 'Gberi and Mittu, west of M'volo. Mittu call themselves Wetu and speak a dialect of Gberi (related to the language of Morokodo and Biti)' and 'Bongo is related to the languages of the Baka, Mittu, 'Beli, Sopi, and other peoples'. The only tone statement in the book concerns Zande.
